(Sūrat al-Aḥzāb is Madanī, and it has seventy-three verses.)

﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾. Addressing him ﷺ with the title of prophethood is an honouring of his station and an alerting to the loftiness of his rank. What is meant by "taqwā" (God-consciousness) that he is commanded to do is steadfastness in it and increasing in it, for it has a wide door and a broad expanse whose extent cannot be reached.

﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who openly profess disbelief,

﴿and the hypocrites﴾, those who conceal it, i.e., in matters that would lead to weakness in the religion and to conceding a lowly position among the Muslims. It is narrated that Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl and Abū al-Aʿwar al-Sulamī came to him ﷺ during the truce that existed between him ﷺ and them, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr and al-Jadd ibn Qays stood with them and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Abandon mention of our gods, and say that they intercede and benefit, and we will leave you and your Lord." This grieved the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, and they resolved to kill them, and this verse was revealed. That is: fear Allah regarding the breaking of the covenant and the abandoning of the truce, and do not assist the disbelievers of Makkah and the hypocrites of Madīnah in what they request of you.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, exceedingly so in knowledge and wisdom, so He knows all things, of benefits and harms, and therefore He does not command you except with what contains benefit, nor forbid you except from what contains harm, and He does not judge except by what wise purpose demands. Thus the clause is a justification for the command, and the prohibition emphasizes the obligation of complying with both.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 2:

﴿Wa-ittabi'] means: in everything you do and everything you leave undone of the matters of the religion.

﴿what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾: of the verses, among which is this verse commanding the fear of God (taqwa) and forbidding assistance to the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyya) to emphasise the obligation of complying with the command.

﴿Indeed God is ever, of what you do, Well-Acquainted﴾: It has been said: the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the plural is for magnification. It has also been said: it is addressed to him (ﷺ) and to the believers. It has been said: it is addressed to absent persons by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and its remoteness is not hidden. Indeed, it is permissible that the whole be on a kind of taghlib (predominance of one group within a collective address). In any case, the sentence is a reason for the command and an emphasis of its requirement. As for the first two views: it is by way of encouragement and warning, as if it were said: God is well-acquainted with what you do of compliance and of its abandonment, so He will assign to each of them its recompense, reward and punishment. As for the last view: it is by way of encouragement only, as if it were said: God is well-acquainted with what both groups do, so He will guide you to what is good for your condition and the ordering of your affairs, and will inform you of the schemes and corruptions they perform, and will command you with what you should do in repelling and turning them back. Thus there is no escape from following the revelation and acting upon its requirement, definitively.

**(p. 90)** ﴿And put your trust in God⦈ — that is, entrust all your affairs to Him.

﴿And God suffices as a Guardian⦈ — a Protector to whom all affairs are entrusted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 4:

﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body.﴾ This begins the revelation that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow. It is a parable that Allah, exalted is He, struck as a preparation for what follows it, His words: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons.﴾ It is also a warning that the one who is subjected to zihar being a mother, and the adopted child being a son, meaning: they stand in the position of mother and son with respect to the known effects and rulings among them, is impossible, like the gathering of two hearts in one body. It has been said: this is a rejection of the Arab belief that the intelligent and astute man has two hearts. For this reason it was said of Abu Ma'mar, or of Jamil ibn Sayyid al-Fihri: "the one with two hearts." That is, Allah, exalted is He, has not combined two hearts in one man. The mention of the "body" (jawf) is for the sake of emphasis, as in His words: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.﴾ There is no wifehood or motherhood in a woman, and no claim or sonship in a person, but not in the sense of negating the combination of the real essence of wifehood and motherhood, or negating the combination of the real essence of claim and sonship, as with the heart. Nor in the sense of negating the combination of the rulings of wifehood and the rulings of motherhood, or negating the combination of the rulings of claim and the rulings of sonship absolutely. Rather, it means negating the combination of the real essence of wifehood with the rulings of motherhood, and negating the combination of the real essence of claim with the rulings of sonship, in order to nullify what they used to do: applying the rulings of motherhood to the one subjected to zihar, and applying the rulings of sonship to the adopted child.

The meaning of "zihar" (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother") is that one says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." It is derived from "the back" (zahr) in terms of the wording, like the talbiyah (the call "labbayk") from labbayk. It is construed with "min" because it includes the meaning of abstaining; it was a form of divorce in the pre-Islamic period, and in Islam it requires either divorce or prohibition, until the kaffarah (expiation) is paid, just as the verb "ala" (to swear abstention) is construed with it, and it has the meaning of "halafa" (to swear). The mention of "zihar" is a metaphor for the belly, which is its pillar, since mentioning it is close to mentioning the private parts; or it is for the sake of intensifying the prohibition, since they used to forbid intercourse with the wife while her back was turned toward the sky.

It is read: (اللّاءِ), and it is read: (تُظاهِرُونَ) with one of the two tas elided, from تَتَظاهَرُونَ and تَظّاهَرُونَ with the second tā' assimilated into the ẓā'; and (تُظْهِرُونَ) from أظهر with the meaning of تظهر; and (تَظْهَرُونَ) from ظَهَرَ, with the meaning of ظاهَرَ, like عَقَدَ meaning عاقَدَ; and (تَظْهَرُونَ) from ظَهَرَ ظُهُورًا.

Adiya' (أدْعِياء) is the plural of da'iy (دَعِيّ), the one who is claimed as a son (the adopted child). This plural is irregular, since afila' (أفْعِلاء) is specific to فَعِيل in the sense of فاعل, like تَقِيّ and أتْقِياء. It was as if it were made to resemble it in wording, so it was given its plural, like قُتَلاء and أُسَراء.

﴿That﴾ refers to what is understood from what has been mentioned of zihar and claiming, or to the last, which is the intended subject of the discourse, meaning: your claiming by your saying, "This is my son."

﴿Is merely your saying with your mouths﴾, without there being any reality or actual existence in external things corresponding to it. Therefore it is far removed from entailing the rulings of sonship, as you claim.

﴿But Allah speaks the truth﴾ that corresponds to reality, ﴿and He guides to the way﴾, meaning the way of truth and nothing else. So leave your sayings, and take hold of His words, mighty and majestic is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 5:

﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾. That is: attribute them to their fathers (p-91) and specify them by them. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ is a justification for it, and the pronoun refers to the verbal noun of "call" (ud'u), as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾. "Aqsat" is an elative (af'al) intended for the sheer increase of quality, from al-qist (justice), meaning: calling them by their fathers' names is far more consummate in justice and truthfulness in the judgment and decree of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And if you do not know their fathers﴾, so that you may attribute them to them.

﴿Then they are your brothers in religion and your clients (mawali)﴾: then they are your brothers in religion and your allies in it. That is: call them by religious brotherhood and clientage (mawlawiyyah).

﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, no sin, ﴿for what you have erred in﴾, that is, for what you did of that while being mistaken, through forgetfulness, oblivion, or a slip of the tongue.

﴿But what your hearts have intended﴾: that is, but the blame lies in what your hearts intended after the prohibition, or in what your hearts intended as sinful in it.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾: for His pardon of the one who errs, and the ruling on adoption, by his saying, "He is my son," when the one who speaks it is a slave, freedom applies in every case; and his lineage is not established from him except when he is of unknown lineage, and the like of him could be born to the like of the adopter, and he had not previously acknowledged his lineage from another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 6:

﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾. That is: in every matter of the religion and of the worldly life, as the unrestricted wording attests. It is therefore obligatory that he (ﷺ) be more beloved to them than their own selves, his judgment more binding upon them than their own judgment, his right more preferred by them than their own rights, and their compassion for him more prior than their compassion for themselves. It is related that he (ﷺ) intended the expedition of Tabuk and commanded the people to set out, and some people said: "We will seek permission from our fathers and our mothers." Then this was revealed. And it was recited: "and he is a father to them", that is, in religion, for every prophet is a father to his community in that he is the root of that by which eternal life is attained, and for this reason the believers became brothers.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾. That is: they are placed in the station of mothers with regard to prohibition (of marriage) and deserving of honour. As for other matters beyond that, they are like non-related women. For this reason 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "We are not the mothers of (the) women."

﴿And those of blood relationship﴾. That is: those who have kinship.

﴿are nearer to one another﴾ in inheritance. This abrogates what was in the early period of Islam regarding inheritance by emigration and allegiance in religion.

﴿in the Book of Allah﴾. In the Preserved Tablet, or in what He revealed. That is this verse, or the verse of inheritance, or what Allah the Exalted has prescribed.

﴿of the believers and the emigrants﴾. An explanation of "those of blood relationship", or a complement of "nearer" (awla), meaning: those of blood relationship, by the right of kinship, are nearer for inheritance than the believers by the right of religion, and than the emigrants by the right of emigration.

﴿except that you do a kindness to your allies﴾. An exception from the most general thing in which nearness may be estimated regarding benefit; the meaning of doing a kindness is bequest. Or it is a disjunctive exception.

﴿That was written in the Book as a decree﴾. That is: what was mentioned of the two verses was established in the Tablet or in the Qur'an. It was said: in the Torah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 7:

﴿And [remember] when We took from the Prophets their covenant﴾. That is: remember the time when We took from all the Prophets their pledges to convey the Message and to call to the true religion.

﴿and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus the son of Mary﴾. Singling them out for mention, although they are clearly included among the Prophets (indindrajihim fi al-nabiyyin indirajan bayyinan), serves to signal (li-l-idhan) their greater excellence and merit, and that they are among the most renowned bearers of revealed laws and the pillars of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm). The mention of our Prophet first before them, upon them be prayers and peace, serves to manifest his exalted station.

﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾. That is: a covenant of great importance, or one confirmed by oath. This is the very same first covenant, and its taking is their taking; the conjunction (al-'atf) is based on treating the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence, in order to magnify its importance, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾, following His words: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us﴾. And His words, Exalted is He:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 8:**

﴿That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ is connected (*muta'alliq*) to an implied verb (*mudmar*) in a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnaf*), brought in to explain what motivates the mention of taking the covenant (*mithaq*). It is the purpose (*ghaya*) of that verb, not of "We took" (*akhadhna*). The intended point is to remind of the covenant itself, and then to state its purpose explicitly, as the shift of style by *iltifat* (the change from direct address to the third person, *al-ghayba*) indicates. The meaning is: God did that so that on the Day of Resurrection He would ask the Prophets. The expression *al-sadiqin* (the truthful) is placed in the position of their pronoun (*damir*) to signal from the outset that they are truthful in what they are asked about. The questioning is for a wisdom that requires it, namely: so that He asks the Prophets who were true to their pledge about what they said to their peoples, or about the confirmation (*taṣdiq*) they gave to them, as a rebuke to them (*tabkitan lahum*), as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when God gathers the Messengers and says, "What response did you receive?"﴾ (5:109). Or [He asks] those who confirmed them about their confirmation, for the confirmer of the truthful is truthful, and his confirmation is truth.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: so that He asks the believers who were true to their pledge, when He made them witness against themselves, about the truthfulness of their pledge, this is rejected by the context of reminding of the covenant of the Prophets. His saying: ﴿and He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ is conjoined to the implied verb mentioned, not to "We took," as has been said. The explanation that the sending of the Messengers and the taking of the covenant from them was for rewarding the believers, or that the meaning is that God, exalted is He, enjoined upon the Prophets the call to His religion in order to reward the believers, is an evident forced interpretation (*taʿassuf*), since it leads to the statement of the preparation of the painful punishment for the disbelievers not being intended in itself. Yes, it is permissible to conjoin it to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿That He may ask the truthful﴾, as if it were said: "Then He rewarded the believers, and ﴿He has prepared for the disbelievers﴾ ... the verse."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 9:

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ The noun "favor" (ni'mah) is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), so the prepositional phrase "upon you" (alaykum) is connected to it. Otherwise it is connected to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, meaning: existing upon you.

﴿when there came to you armies﴾ This is an adverbial of time (zarf) relating to the favor itself, or to its being established for them. It was also said that it is in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkurū), as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the favor of Allah." By "armies" (junud) are meant the confederates (al-ahzab), namely the Quraysh, Ghatafan, and the Jews of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir. They numbered about twelve thousand. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of their approach, he dug the trench around Medina on the advice of Salman al-Farisi. Then he went out with three thousand of the Muslims, pitched his camp with the trench between himself and the people, and ordered the children and women to be lifted up into the fortresses (al-atam). Fear intensified, the believers thought every kind of thought, and hypocrisy showed itself among the hypocrites — until Mu'attib ibn Qushayr said: "Muhammad used to promise us the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, while none of us can manage to go out to relieve himself." About a month passed for both parties with no fighting between them, except that some horsemen of Quraysh, among them Amr ibn Abd Wudd, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Nawfal ibn Abd Allah, Dirar ibn al-Khattab, and Mirdas, brother of Banu Muharib, mounted their horses and made for a narrow place in the trench, struck their horses, and plunged across. The horses wheeled with them in the marshy ground between the trench and Sal'. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, went out with a group of Muslims until he blocked the breach through which they had crossed. The cavalry then came toward them. Amr was known for his bravery, and he had marked himself so that his place would be seen. Ali said to him: "O Amr, I call you to Allah, His Messenger, and Islam." He said: "I have no need of that; I call you to single combat." He said: "O son of my brother, by Allah, I do not wish to kill you." Ali said: "But by Allah, I wish to kill you." Amr then grew angry, for he was a fierce man famed for courage, leapt down from his horse, hamstrung it, or struck its face, and then turned upon Ali. They grappled and fought hand to hand, and Ali struck him a blow that ended his life. When he killed him, his horsemen fled until they plunged back into the trench in flight. Along with Amr, Ali also killed two men: Munabbih ibn Uthman ibn Abd al-Dar, and Nawfal ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi. It was also said that there was no fighting between them beyond the exchange of arrows and stones, until Allah the Exalted sent down victory. This is His saying, the Exalted:

﴿So We sent upon them a wind﴾ This is conjoined (atf) to "came to you" and is presented to explain the favor in summary; its remainder will come at the end of the story.

﴿and armies you did not see﴾ These were the angels, peace be upon them, and they numbered a thousand. Allah sent upon them a cold east wind on a wintry night, which benumbed them, and it threw dust into their faces. He commanded the angels, who uprooted the tent pegs, cut the ropes, extinguished the fires, overturned the cooking pots, and the horses surged against one another. He cast terror into their hearts, and the angels shouted "Allahu akbar" around the sides of their camp. Talihah ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi said: "As for Muhammad, he has already begun with you the magic of the morning; so flee, flee!" They fled without any fighting.

﴿And Allah is ever, of what you do﴾ of digging the trench, and arranging the beginnings of war. It was also said: of your turning to Him and hoping for His bounty. It is also read with the letter ya' (yaʿmalūna, "of what they do"), meaning: of what the disbelievers do, namely of guarding themselves and fighting, or of disbelief and sins.

﴿Seeing.﴾ Therefore He did what He did, of granting you victory over them. The clause is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh) confirming what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 10:

﴿When they came upon you﴾ is a substitute (badal) for: "when they came upon you [ itjāʾatkum ]".

﴿from above you﴾ meaning from the upper part of the valley, from the direction of the east. They were the Banu Ghatafan and those who followed them from the people of Najd. Their leader was 'Uyayna ibn Hisn, and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl was among Hawazin. The Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir joined them.

﴿and from below you﴾ that is, from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west. They were the Quraysh and those who allied with them from the Ahabish, Banu Kinana and the people of Tihama. Their leader was Abu Sufyan, and they numbered ten thousand.

﴿And when the eyes swerved﴾ is a conjunction with what precedes it, included with it in the sense of the reminder: that is, when the eyes turned away from their normal course and deviated from their level of sight, in bewilderment and fixed staring. It is also said: they turned away from everything and did not look at anything except their enemy, because of the intensity of the terror.

﴿and the hearts reached the throats﴾ because the lungs swell from intense fear, so the heart rises with their rise up to the top of the windpipe (al-hanjara), which is the end of the gullet (al-hulqum). It is also said that this is a metaphor for the agitation and pounding of hearts, even though they did not literally reach the throats. The address in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and you were thinking about Allah with various thoughts﴾ is directed to those who openly display faith in general, meaning: you were thinking about Allah, exalted is He, all sorts of different thoughts. The sincere believers with steadfast hearts thought that Allah, exalted is He, would fulfil His promise of raising His religion, as is indicated by what will be related of their saying: ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth﴾ ... the verse. (p-94) Or He was testing them, so they feared slipping, and endurance was weakened; the weak of heart and the hypocrites [thought] what has been related of them, of what holds no good. The clause is conjoined to "swerved". The form of the present tense is for bringing the scene before the mind and to indicate continuity. It is also read as (al-zunūna) without an alif, which is the regular form, and its addition is for the sake of matching the verse endings (fawasil), as it is added in rhyming words (qawafi) of poetry.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 11:

﴿Hunalika﴾ is an adverb of time, or an adverb of place governing what follows it; that is, "at that terrible time," or "at that place of slipping and peril."

﴿Ubtuliya al-mu'minun﴾ means they were treated as those who are tested; thus the sincere (mukhlis) was distinguished from the hypocrite (munafiq), and the firm in faith (rasikh) from the wavering (mutazalzil).

﴿Wa zulzilu zilzalan shadidan﴾ means they were shaken with a severe shaking, from the terror and dread. It is also recited with a fatha on the zay (zalzalan, i.e., "zulzilu" read as "zulzalu").

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 12:**

﴿And when the hypocrites say﴾: it is coordinated (ʿatf) with "when [their eyes] swerved" (idh zaghat). The use of the present tense (ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ) indicates, for the reason already mentioned, the continuity of the saying and the vividness of its depiction (istiḥḍār ṣūratih).

﴿And those in whose hearts is a disease﴾: i.e., weakness of belief.

﴿What Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾: namely, the elevation of the religion and victory.

﴿Except as delusion﴾: i.e., a promise of delusion (waʿd ghurūr). It was also said: a false statement. The one who said it was Muʿattib ibn Qushayr and his like, who were content with it. He said: "Muhammad promises us the conquest of the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, while one of us cannot even relieve himself out of fear. This is nothing but a promise of delusion."

**﴿And when a group of them said﴾** They were Aws ibn Qayzi and his followers. It was also said that they were Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his partisans.

**﴿O people of Yathrib﴾** This is the name of the Radiant City (al-Madinah al-Munawwarah). It was also said that it is the name of a plot of land in which the city lies. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that it be called by this name because he disliked it, and he said: "It is Taybah, or Tabah." It seems they used that name in opposition to him (ﷺ). Calling them by the title of their belonging to it prepares the way for what follows, namely the command to return to it.

**﴿There is no station for you﴾** There is no place of residence for you, or: there is no residence for you here, meaning the encampment. It is also recited with a fatḥah on the mīm, as مَقامَ (maqām), which means: there is no standing for you, or: there is no place of standing for you.

**﴿So return﴾** That is, to your dwellings in Madinah. What they actually meant was an order to flee, but they expressed it as "return" to make their statement appealing and to signal that it was not the blameworthy kind of flight. It was also said that the meaning is: there is no standing for you in the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), so return to what you were upon of polytheism; or return from what you pledged to him and hand him over to his enemies. Or: there is no station for you in Yathrib, so return as unbelievers so that you may be able to remain there. The first interpretation is the most suitable to what follows, for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a party of them asks the Prophet for permission﴾ is coordinated with "said." The use of the present tense conveys the vividness of the scene. They were the Banu Harithah and the Banu Salamah, who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to return, complying with their command. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿saying﴾ is either a substitute for "asks permission," or a circumstantial clause describing its subject, or a resumed statement answering the question about the manner of seeking permission.

**﴿Indeed, our houses are exposed﴾** That is, they are not secure, open to the enemy and to thieves. So grant us permission until we fortify them, then we will return to the army. The word ʿawrah (عَوْرَةٌ) originally means a defect, and it was applied to what is defective as an intensive. It has also been permitted that it be a lightened form of ʿawirah (عَوِرَةٌ), from "the house became defective" when it fell into disrepair, and it has been recited that way. The first meaning is the more suitable to the context of excuse-making, as the opening of their statement with the particle of confirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq, the particle that affirms and asserts) reveals.

**﴿But they are not exposed﴾** while the situation is that they are not so.

**﴿They only intend﴾** what they intend by seeking permission.

**﴿but to flee﴾** from the fighting.

And if it had been entered upon them (﴿وَلَوْ دُخِلَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾): the entering is attributed to their houses and is made to fall upon them, because what is meant is the supposed entry into the houses while they are within them, not the supposed entry into them in general, as the surface meaning would suggest. Had the prepositional phrase not been mentioned, and had the supposed entry upon them not been general, as the surface meaning would suggest. Had it been attributed to the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-al-majrūr, "the prepositional phrase"), [it would read] ﴿from its sides﴾, meaning from all its sides, not from some of them to the exclusion of others. The meaning is: if their houses were completely breached, and everyone who wished from among the people of corruption and mischief entered them, ﴿then they were asked﴾ by another group at that time of calamity and terrifying quaking.

﴿the strife﴾ means: apostasy and a return to disbelief (ridda, "apostasy"), in place of what they were now asked of, namely faith and obedience.

﴿they would have given it﴾ means: they would have granted it, not caring about the great calamity that had befallen them and the fierce raid. It was also read as (لَأتَوْها), with the short vowel form, meaning: they would have done it and come to it.

﴿and they would not have delayed in it﴾, that is, in the strife: they would not have let it remain nor postponed it ﴿except briefly﴾, for only as much time as the question and answer would take, let alone making excuses on account of the disruption of the houses while they remained intact, as they now do. It was said: they would not have remained in Medina after apostasy except briefly, but the first interpretation is the one fitting to this context. As for restricting the imposition of entry to those allied armies, this, together with its conflict with the generality conveyed by omitting the agent of the entering, involves a kind of defect in the arrangement, as you have learned, since the thrust of the noble composition is to explain that when they are called to the truth they make excuses with some trivial matter, but if they are called to falsehood they hasten to it more eagerly than anything, without any restraint turning them back or any inclination holding them back. Therefore, making the imposition of entry upon them come from the mentioned armies, and attributing the asking of the strife and the call to disbelief to another group, while the armies are the known enemies of the religion, those directly engaged in fighting the believers, persistent in turning away from the truth and striving in calling to disbelief and error, is far from being appropriate.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 15:

﴿And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs.﴾ Indeed, the Banu Harithah had made a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, when they lost heart, that they would not return to the like of it. It is also said: they were a people who were absent from the battle of Badr, and they saw what Allah had bestowed upon the people of Badr of honour and excellence, so they said: "If Allah makes us witness a battle, we will surely fight."

﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever answerable.﴾ That is, it is demanded and required, so that it must be fulfilled; and it is also said: it is answerable, meaning they will be questioned about fulfilling it and will be recompensed for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 16:

﴿Say: Flight will never benefit you if you flee from death or killing.﴾ For every person must certainly die a natural death (ḥatf anf), or be killed by the sword, at a specific time that was preceded by the decree (al-qada'), and over which the Pen (al-qalam) has run.

﴿And then you would not be given enjoyment except for a little.﴾ That is: even if flight were to benefit you, for example, and you were given enjoyment through delay, that enjoyment would be only a small enjoyment, or a short period of time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 17:

﴿Say: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm, or intends for you mercy?"﴾ (p-96) That is: or He afflicts you with harm if He intends mercy for you. The speech has been abbreviated; or the second (clause) is understood as governed by the first, because of the sense of prevention (man') inherent in protection ('ismah).

﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any protector (waliyy)﴾ who benefits them, ﴿nor any helper (nasir)﴾ who repels harm from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, Allah knows those among you who hinder (others)﴾, i.e., those who discourage the people from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they are the hypocrites.

﴿And those who say to their brothers﴾ from among the hypocrites of Madinah: ﴿"Come here to us!"﴾ Halumma (halumma) is a sound that has been named as a transitive verb, like: "Attend!" or "Bring yourself near!" It is used identically for the singular and the plural according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, whereas the Banu Tamim say: halumma, ya rajul (to a man), and halummu, ya rijal (to men), meaning: "Bring yourselves near to us." This indicates that at the time of this saying they were coming out of the camp, heading toward Madinah.

﴿And they do not come to the fighting﴾, i.e., the battle and the combat.

﴿except a little﴾, i.e., a little coming, or a little time, or a little fighting. For they make excuses, discourage as much as they are able, and go out with the believers, giving them the impression that they are with them; and you will not see them fighting or engaging in combat except a little, when they are compelled to it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They fought not except a little﴾. It has also been said that this is part of their speech, meaning: "The companions of Muhammad do not go to the battle of the confederates, and they do not confront them except a little."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 19:

﴿Stingy towards you﴾: that is, miserly towards you in aiding (you), or in spending in the way of Allah, or in (sharing) victory and booty. It is the plural of shahih (stingy). Its being in the accusative is either as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of ya'tuna (they come), or of al-mu'awwiqin (those who hinder), or it is in the accusative of censure (al-dhamm).

﴿So when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling﴾: in their eye-sockets.

﴿Like one who is overcome by death﴾: it is an attribute of the verb-noun (masdar) of yanzurun (they look), or a circumstantial state of its subject, or an attribute of the masdar of tadur (roll), or a circumstantial state of their eyes. That is: they look with a look like the look of one who has fainted from the agonies of death, out of fear and cowardice, and clinging to you. Or: they look while being like "the one who..." etc. Or: their eyes roll with a rolling like the rolling of his eye, or their eyes roll being like his eye.

﴿But when fear departs﴾, and the spoils are gathered in, ﴿they will assail you﴾, that is, strike you, ﴿with sharp tongues﴾, and say: Grant us our share, for we have witnessed you, fought alongside you, and by our position you overcame your enemy, and through us you were given victory over it. Al-salq is spreading out (something) by force, with the hand or with the tongue. It is also read: (sala'uukum).

﴿Stingy towards good﴾: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, or of censure, and the reading in the nominative supports it.

﴿Those﴾: the ones described with the bad attributes mentioned, ﴿they have not believed﴾ with sincerity, ﴿so Allah has nullified their deeds﴾: that is, He has shown their nullity, since they had no deeds that could be established and thus made void; or He has nullified their pretence and hypocrisy, so that nothing remained that would bring any worldly benefit at all.

﴿And that﴾ nullification ﴿is ever easy for Allah﴾: easy, effortless. The singling out of its ease for mention, although everything is easy for Him, exalted is He, is to show that their deeds are truly deserving that their nullification should appear, given the complete convergence of motives and the total absence of deterrents.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 20:

﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾. That is: these (hypocrites), out of their cowardice (p-97), suppose that the confederates have not been routed, so they fled to the inside of the city.

﴿And if the confederates should come [again]﴾ a second time ﴿they would wish that they were [out] in the desert among the Bedouins﴾, meaning they would wish they were outside, in the open country, among the Arabs (a-'a'rab). It is also read as (buddan), the plural of (badin), like (ghazin) and (ghuzzan).

﴿They would ask﴾ every arrival from the direction of the city. It is also read as (yassa'alun), meaning (yatasa'alun), "they ask one another." Its meaning is that some of them say to others: "What did you hear? What has reached you?" Or they ask the Bedouins, as one says: "I saw the crescent and we saw it together (tara'aynahu)," for the form of reciprocity (tafa'ul) may be stripped of the meaning of the subject being both agent and object in some respect, and it is sufficient that there be more than one agent, as in the example mentioned and its like.

﴿About your news﴾, that is, about what has happened to you. ﴿And even if they were among you﴾ this time, and had not returned to the city, and there were fighting,

﴿they would not have fought except a little﴾, out of ostentation and fear of reproach.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 21:

﴿Certainly you have in the Messenger of God an excellent example﴾ an excellent quality, which is worthy of being emulated, such as steadfastness in war and enduring hardships. Or it means that he himself is an example worthy of being followed, as when you say: "In the egg are twenty mans of iron" (man, a unit of weight), meaning that the egg itself contains this amount of iron. It is also read with a kasra on the hamza (ʾiswatun, rather than ʾuswatun), and this is a dialectal form of the same word.

﴿for him who hopes in God and the Last Day﴾ meaning: hopes for the reward of God, or for His meeting, or specifically the Days of God and the Last Day. It is said that this is like your saying: "I hope for Zayd and his bounty," since the Last Day is among the days of God the Exalted. The phrase "for him who" (li-man kana) is either a complement (ṣilah) modifying "an excellent [example]," or a qualifier (ṣifah) of it. It is also said that it is a substitute (badal) for "for you" (lakum), though most grammarians hold that a pronoun of the addressee cannot be substituted by a noun.

﴿and remembers God﴾ meaning: and he couples hope with the remembrance of God.

﴿often﴾ meaning: a great deal of remembrance, or a long period of time, for persistence in remembering God the Exalted leads to constant obedience, and through this the emulation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is realized.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 22:

﴿When the believers saw the confederates⦆ is an explanation of what issued from the sincere believers at the confusion of affairs and the divergence of opinions, after the narration of what issued from others; that is, when they witnessed them as they had been described to them.

﴿They said, "This is..."⦆ pointing to what they had witnessed, in terms of its being the thing itself, without any word denoting it occurring to their minds, let alone its masculine or feminine form, for these are properties of the word. As was mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord."⦆ and he (Abraham) made it a reference to the calamity or the trial, as a result of the noble contemplation; so reflect. Yes, it is permissible to use the masculine form in view of the predicate, which is ﴿what Allah and His Messenger promised us⦆, for that is the first thing that occurs to their minds at the moment of witnessing. Their intention by that is what they had been promised by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them...⦆ up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.⦆ And by his (ﷺ) saying: "The matter will become severe with the confederates gathering against you, but the final outcome will be yours over them." And by his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed the confederates will march against you after nine or ten nights." It was also read with a kasra on the ra' and a fatha on the hamza.

﴿And Allah and His Messenger spoke truly⦆ that is, the truth of the report of Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger became manifest; or they both spoke truly in regard to the help and the reward, just as they spoke truly regarding the trial. The explicit mention of the Name is for glorification.

﴿And it increased them not⦆ that is, what they saw.

﴿except in faith⦆ in Allah, exalted is He, and in His promises.

(p-98)﴿and in submission⦆ to His commands and His decrees.

**﴿Among the believers﴾**: that is, those who believed sincerely, in general, not only those whose virtues are specifically related here.

**﴿men who were true to what they covenanted with God﴾** concerning steadfastness alongside the Messenger (ﷺ) and fighting against the enemies of the religion. These were men from among the Companions (may God be pleased with them). They vowed that if they met battle alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ), they would stand firm and fight until they were martyred. They were ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbaydillāh, Saʿīd ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Ḥamzah, Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr, Anas ibn al-Naḍr, and others, may the good pleasure of God Most High be upon them all.

The meaning of "ṣadaqū" (were true) is that they brought truthfulness, from the expression "ṣadaqanī" when one says to you the truth. The grammatical position (i'rab) of "mā ʿāhadū" (what they covenanted) is in the accusative case, and this may be either by dropping the preposition from it so that the verb reaches it directly, as in their saying "ṣadaqanī sinna bakrihi" (he told me the truth about the age of his young camel), meaning "in its age". Or the object of the covenant may be treated figuratively as something that was made true, as if they addressed him in the manner of one who says to his generous friends:

*"The enemies have slaughtered me, if you will not slaughter [for me]"*

They said to him: "We will be true to you." And since they fulfilled it, they were true to him. Had they broken it, they would have been called liars, and it would have been a lie.

**﴿Among them is one who has fulfilled his vow﴾** is a detailing of the state of the truthful ones, and a division of them into two categories. "Naḥb" means a vow, which is that a person binds himself to some act of his and makes it obligatory upon himself. Its fulfilment is completion of it and keeping it. The grammatical position of the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa al-majrūr) is nominative, as the subject of an inchoative sentence (mubtadaʾ), according to one of the two possibilities mentioned in God's saying: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God"﴾ ... the verse. That is: "So some of them," or "So some of them is one who has fulfilled [his vow]," such as Ḥamzah, Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr, Anas ibn al-Naḍr (the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Mālik), and others, may the good pleasure of God Most High be upon them all. They have indeed completed their vows, whether the vow is taken in its literal sense, namely that what they vowed was their voluntary acts, which is fighting, limited by what is not part of it, and it does not fall under the vow, which is death as a martyr; or the vow was used figuratively, by binding themselves to what will be mentioned.

**﴿And among them﴾**: that is, and some of them, or and some from among them.

**﴿is one who awaits﴾**: that is, the fulfilment of his vow, because it is time-bound, like ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, and others who were martyred after that, may the good pleasure of God Most High be upon them all. They are continuing in their vows, having fulfilled part of them, which is steadfastness alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and fighting until the time of the revelation of this noble verse, and they are awaiting the fulfilment of the remaining part of it, which is fighting until death as martyrs. Moreover, it is permissible that "naḥb" be used figuratively for binding oneself to death as a martyr, either by treating the binding to its causes, which are voluntary acts for the one making the vow, as if it were the binding itself, or by treating the binding itself as if it were its causes and attributing the binding to it. The latter is more fitting to the context of praise. In any case, describing them with "awaiting," which indicates desire for what is awaited, is a true testimony to the completeness of their longing for martyrdom. As for what has been said, that "naḥb" was borrowed for death because it is like a binding vow upon the neck of every living being, this is a distortion of the figure of speech, a removal of its splendour, and a removal of the noble composition from the demands of the context entirely.

**﴿And they did not change﴾**: a conjunction with "ṣadaqū" (were true), and its subject is its subject, that is: and they did not alter their covenant or change it.

**﴿in any change﴾**: that is, not a change in any way, neither in essence nor in attribute. Rather, they remained steadfast in it, desiring it, observing its rights in the best manner. As for those who fulfilled their vows, it is evident. As for the rest, their waiting bears witness to it in the most truthful testimony. The generalization of "not changing" to the first group, despite the clarity of their condition, is to indicate that the second group is equal to them in the ruling. (p-99) It is also permissible that the pronoun in "baddalū" (they changed) refers specifically to those who are awaiting, on the basis that what needed clarification was their state. It has been narrated that "Ṭalḥa (may God be pleased with him) remained steadfast alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Uḥud until his hand was struck, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Ṭalḥa has made Paradise obligatory.'" In another narration: "Ṭalḥa has made [it] obligatory." And from him (ﷺ), in a narration of Jābir (may God be pleased with him): "Whoever would be pleased to look at a martyr walking on the earth, let him look at Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbaydillāh." And in a narration of ʿĀʾishah (may God be pleased with her): "Whoever would be pleased to look at a martyr walking on the earth, who has fulfilled his vow, let him look at Ṭalḥa." This indicates that he is, in ruling, among the first group.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 24:

﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness﴾ is connected to a suppressed (implied) verb, a resumptive clause (mustanaf) brought in the manner of a summary (fadhlaka) to explain what prompts the occurrence of the states and statements narrated in detail. It is also its ultimate purpose (ghayah), as passed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾. It is as if it were said: all that occurred happened so that Allah may reward the truthful for what proceeded from them of truthfulness and fidelity, in word and in deed.

﴿And punish the hypocrites﴾ for the deeds and statements narrated that proceeded from them.

﴿If He wills﴾ to punish them, ﴿or turn to them in mercy﴾ if they repent. It has been said: it is connected to what precedes it, namely the explicit negation of change (tabdil) and its implicit affirmation through allusion, as if the hypocrites intended by changing the evil outcome, just as the sincere believers intended by steadfastness and fidelity the good outcome. It has been said: it is a causal explanation of "they were truthful." It has been said: it is due to what is understood from His words, exalted is He: "And it only increased them in faith and submission." It has been said: it is due to what is derived from His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates﴾, as if it were said: Allah tested them by seeing that tremendous affair ﴿so that He may reward﴾ ... the verse. So reflect, and success is from Allah.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, i.e., to whoever repents. This is a parenthetical clause containing an incitement to repentance. And His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 25:

﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved﴾ is a return to narrating the rest of the story, and an elaboration of the completion of the blessing referred to in summary by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We sent against them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾. It is coordinated either with the implied element assumed before His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that Allah may reward﴾, as if it were said, after narrating the matters mentioned, "What happened of the events occurred." 

﴿And Allah turned back﴾ ... etc. Or it is coordinated with "We sent" (arsalna), and between them has been inserted an explanation that what descended upon them was a catastrophic event by which intellects and understandings were bewildered, and a complete calamity by which knees rubbed together and feet slipped. It also elaborates what proceeded from the two groups, the people of faith and the people of disbelief and hypocrisy, of states and statements, in order to show the greatness of the blessing and to make clear its noble value by explaining that it reached them at the extreme of their need for it. That is: So We sent against them a wind and hosts you did not see, and by that We turned back those who disbelieved. The turn to the noble Name is to cultivate awe and to instill dread. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in their rage﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun, meaning: being afflicted with it. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they did not obtain any good﴾, either by overlapping or by succession, meaning: not succeeding in any good; or the second is an explanation of the first; or it is a resumptive new clause.

﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ by what has been mentioned of sending the wind and the hosts.

﴿And Allah is ever Powerful﴾ over bringing about whatever He wills.

﴿Exalted in Might﴾ (p-100) prevailing over everything.

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who had supported them﴾ — that is, those who aided the confederates who had been repulsed.

﴿from their fortresses﴾ — from their strongholds. The singular is ṣayṣiyah, meaning that by which one fortifies oneself; hence the horn of a bull or gazelle and the spur of a rooster are also called ṣayṣiyah.

﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ — intense fear, such that they surrendered themselves to be killed, and their women and children to be taken captive, as His words indicate: ﴿a party you slew and a party you took captive﴾, without any movement on their part, let alone opposition or defiance. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the morning of the night in which the confederates were routed, the Muslims had returned to Madinah, and they had put down their weapons. He said: "Are you laying down your armour while the angels have not laid down their weapons? Allah commands you to march against Banu Qurayzah, and I am heading toward them. So proclaim to the people that none should pray the ʿAsr prayer except at Banu Qurayzah." They besieged them for twenty-one or twenty-five nights, until the siege exhausted them. He said to them: "Will you come down under my judgment?" They refused. He said: "Under the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh?" They agreed to it. Saʿd judged that their fighting men should be killed and their offspring and women taken captive. The Prophet (ﷺ) said "Takbir" and said: "You have judged by the judgment of Allah from above the seven heavens." He killed six hundred fighting men, and it was said: between eight hundred and nine hundred; and he took seven hundred captive.

It was also read as (تَأْسُرُونَ) with a dammah on the sīn, just as (الرُّعُبَ) was read with a dammah on the ʿayn. Perhaps the postponement of the object in the second clause, although the flow of speech is for its detailing and division, is as in His words: ﴿so a party you denied and a party you kill﴾ and His words: ﴿a party they denied and a party they kill﴾, for the sake of the verse-endings (fawāṣil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 27:

﴿And He caused you to inherit their land and their homes﴾, i.e., their fortresses.

﴿And their wealth﴾, including their money (nuqud), their household goods (athath), and their livestock (mawashi). It is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave their property (aqar) to the Muhajirun to the exclusion of the Ansar. The Ansar said about that..." Then he (ﷺ) said: "You have your dwellings." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Will you not set aside a fifth (takhmis) as you did on the Day of Badr?" He (ﷺ) said: "No, this was given to me as a special provision (tu'mah) apart from the people." They said: "We are content with what Allah and His Messenger have done."

﴿And land you had not trodden﴾, i.e., He caused you to inherit, in His knowledge and decree, land you had not yet taken possession of, such as that of Persia and Rome. It was also said: every land that will be conquered until the Day of Resurrection. And it was said: Khaybar.

﴿And Allah is ever, over all things, Competent﴾. You have witnessed some of His decrees in the inheritance of the lands you have taken possession of, so draw an analogy from them to whatever lies beyond them.

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: if you desire the life of this world﴾, that is, its ease and luxury.

﴿and its adornment﴾, that is, its ornaments.

﴿then come [فَتَعالَيْنَ]﴾, that is, come forward by your own will and choice to one of the two options, as one says "he came to argue with me" (أقْبَلَ يُخاصِمُنِي), "he went to speak with me" (ذَهَبَ يُكَلِّمُنِي), and "he stood to threaten me" (قامَ يُهَدِّدُنِي).

﴿I will provide for you [أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ]﴾, with the jussive (بِالجَزْمِ) as a response to the imperative. Likewise ﴿and release you [وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ]﴾, that is, I will give you the mut'ah (a provision or gift of consolation) and divorce you.

﴿a graceful release [سَراحًا جَمِيلا]﴾, a divorce without harm. It is also read in the nominative (بِالرَّفْعِ), as a resumed sentence (عَلى الِاسْتِئْنافِ). It is reported that they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for garments of adornment and an increase in maintenance, so this was revealed. He began with Aisha and offered her the choice, and she chose Allah, His Messenger, and the Hereafter. Then the rest chose as she had chosen, and Allah praised them for that. Then it was revealed: ﴿Women are not lawful for you hereafter﴾.

There is a difference of opinion as to whether this offer of choice was a delegation of divorce to them, such that the divorce would take effect by the very act of choosing, or not. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and most of the scholars held that it was not a delegation of divorce, but only an offer of choice between the two desires, on the basis that if they desired the world, he (ﷺ) would separate from them. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿then come, I will provide for you and release you﴾. Others held that it was a delegation of divorce to them, so that if they chose themselves, that would be a divorce.

Similarly, there is a difference regarding the ruling on the offer of choice. Ibn Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, said: if a man gives his wife the choice and she chooses her husband, nothing at all takes effect. If she chooses herself, it is one irrevocable divorce (طَلْقَةً بائِنَةً) according to us, and a revocable divorce (رَجْعِيَّةً) according to al-Shafi'i. This is also the view of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Ibn Abi Layla, and Sufyan. It is reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that if she chooses her husband, one divorce takes effect, and if she chooses herself, three divorces take effect; this is the view of al-Hasan and a report from Malik. It is reported from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that if she chooses her husband, it is one revocable divorce, and if she chooses herself, one irrevocable divorce. It is also reported from him that if she chooses her husband, nothing at all takes effect, and this is the consensus of the jurists of the major cities.

It has been reported from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave us the choice, and we chose him, and he did not count it as a divorce."

Placing the mut'ah before the release is a matter of generosity, and in it there is a cutting off of their excuses from the outset. The mut'ah for a divorced woman who has not been consummated and for whom no dowry was fixed at the contract is obligatory according to us, and for the others it is recommended (مُسْتَحَبَّةٌ). It consists of a shirt (دِرْعٌ), a head-covering (خِمارٌ), and a wrap (مِلْحَفَةٌ), in accordance with one's means of ease or constraint, except that if half of her dowry is less than that, then the lesser of the two becomes obligatory for her, and it must not be less than five dirhams.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 29:

﴿And if you desire Allah and His Messenger﴾ That is: if you desire His Messenger. The mention of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is for the purpose of announcing the exalted station of his (ﷺ) position with Him, may He be exalted.

﴿And the Last Abode﴾ That is: its bliss, before which there is no value whatsoever for this world and all that is in it.

﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you﴾ in return for their good conduct.

﴿a great reward﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated and whose extent cannot be reached. The "min" (مِن) here is for specification (al-tabyin), because all of them are good-doers. The stripping of the first conditional clause from any threat is for the sake of emphasizing the realization of the meaning of choice (al-takhyir) and guarding against any trace of compulsion. This is the secret behind what is mentioned concerning placing the giving of provision (al-tamti') before the release (al-tasrih), and in describing the release as "beautiful" (bil-jamil).

O women of the Prophet (ﷺ)! [This is a] shift in address, directing the speech to them to show concern for advising them. Their being addressed here, and in what follows, by their connection to him (ﷺ) is because it is he (ﷺ) around whom the rulings that concern them revolve.

﴿Whoever of you commits a flagrant indecency﴾ (bi-fāḥishatin mubayyinatin), i.e., a grave sin, ﴿manifestly ugly﴾ (mubayyinah), from bayyana in the sense of tabayyana (to become manifest). It is also read with a fatḥah on the yā' (mubayyinah). What is meant by it is every grave sin they commit. It has also been said that it refers to their disobedience to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), their defiance (nushūz), and their asking of him for what burdens him, or what straitens his patience and grieves him on their account. It is also read as (ta'ti) with the feminine second-person prefix.

﴿Its punishment will be doubled for her, double﴾, i.e., they will be punished with twice the punishment of others, that is, double its equivalent, because the sin from them is more heinous. The increase in its heinousness follows the increase in the offender's merit and in the favor bestowed upon him. For this reason the prescribed penalty for a free woman was made double that for a slave, and the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, were rebuked for things for which the (ordinary) communities are not rebuked. It is also read as (yuḍ‘af) in the passive voice, and as (yuḍā‘af) and (nuḍ‘if) with the nūn of majesty in the active voice, with the punishment in the accusative.

﴿And that is easy for God﴾: the fact that they are the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) does not prevent Him from doubling it; rather, it calls for it, in consideration of his right.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 31:

﴿Whoever among you (wives of the Prophet) is obedient to Allah and His Messenger, and does righteous deeds﴾ It is also read with the (feminine) ta' (i.e., "taqnut"), meaning: whoever persists in obedience to ﴿Allah and His Messenger, and does righteous deeds, We will give her her reward twice﴾: once for obedience and piety, and a second time for her seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through contentment and good companionship. It is also read as (yaʿmal) with the (masculine) ya', taking it in agreement with the wording of "man" (whoever), and (yuʾtihā) so that in it there is a pronoun referring to the Name of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿And We have prepared for her﴾ in Paradise, in addition to her doubled reward,

﴿a generous provision﴾, that is, one that is pleasing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 32:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women﴾. The original root of aḥad (anyone, any one) is waḥd, in the sense of "one." It was then placed in negation, where it applies equally to the masculine and the feminine, to the singular and the plural. The meaning is: you are not like a single group among the groups of women in excellence and nobility.

﴿If you fear God﴾: that is, if you avoid opposing the command of God Most High and the pleasure of His Messenger; or, if you are characterized by taqwa (God-consciousness), as is fitting for your station.

﴿So do not be soft in speech﴾: when addressing people, that is, do not answer with a speech that is submissive and gentle in the manner of the speech of women who arouse suspicion and of women of loose conduct.

﴿Lest he in whose heart is a disease should be tempted﴾: that is, wickedness and suspicion. It has been read with jazm (the jussive), as a conjunction with the place of the prohibitive verb (lā takhḍa'na), on the basis that it is a prohibition to the one with a diseased heart from desiring, following their prohibition of inciting desire through submissive speech. It is as if it were said: "Do not be submissive in speech, so that the one with a diseased heart will not desire."

﴿And speak a good word﴾: far from suspicion, and from arousing desire, with seriousness and roughness, without softening (of tone); or, a good word even though it is rough.

﴿And stay in your houses﴾ is an imperative from قَرَّ (qarra), yaqarru, of the pattern عَلِمَ (ʿalima). Its original form is اقْرُرْنَ (iqrurna). The first راء (rāʾ) was deleted, and its vowel fatḥa was transferred to the letter before it, as in your saying ظَلْنَ (ẓalna). Alternatively, it is from قارَ (qāra), yaqāru, meaning "to gather." It has also been read with a kasra on the qāf, from وَقَرَ (waqara), yaqiru, wiqāran, meaning "to remain firm and settle." Its original form is أوْقِرْنَ (awqirna), and it underwent the same treatment as بَعُدْنَ (baʿudna) from وَعَدَ (waʿada). Or it is from قِرِيَقَرَ (qirīqarra), where one of the two rāʾs of اقْرُرْنَ was deleted and its kasra was moved to the qāf, as you say ظَلْنَ.

﴿And do not display yourselves immodestly﴾: that is, do not strut about in your walking.

﴿like the display of the first Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance)﴾: that is, a display like the display of women in the earlier Jahiliyyah, which is the period between Adam and Noah. It was said: it is the period between Idris and Noah, peace be upon them both. It was also said: it is the time in which Abraham was born, when a woman would wear her armour of pearls and walk in the middle of the road, presenting herself to men. It was also said: it is the time of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both. The other Jahiliyyah is the period between ʿIsa and Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them both. It was also said: the first Jahiliyyah is the Jahiliyyah of disbelief, and the other Jahiliyyah is wickedness within Islam. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu al-Darda', "Indeed, there is in you a Jahiliyyah." He asked, "Is it a Jahiliyyah of disbelief or a Jahiliyyah of Islam?" He said, "Rather, it is a Jahiliyyah of disbelief."(p-103)

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: they were commanded with these two because they are superior to other acts, and because they are the foundations of bodily and financial acts of obedience.

﴿And obey God and His Messenger﴾: that is, in all that you do and all that you refrain from, especially in what you have been commanded and forbidden.

﴿God only desires to remove from you the defilement, O people of the household﴾: that is, the sin that stains your honour. This is a justification for their commands and prohibitions, given as a new independent clause. For this reason the ruling was generalised by addressing others besides them, and the intended meaning was stated explicitly, either by the form of address or by praise.

﴿people of the household﴾: meaning those whom the House of Prophethood encompasses.

﴿and purify you﴾: from the filth of sins and transgressions.

﴿with a thorough purification﴾: The word الرِّجْس (rijs, defilement) is used metaphorically for disobedience, and the word التَّطْهِير (taṭhīr, purification) is used as a complement to heighten the aversion to it. This verse, as you see, is a clear proof and a bright argument that the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) are among his household. It refutes the view of the Shiʿa (the Shiʿah), who restrict the people of the household to Fatima, ʿAli, and their two sons, may God be pleased with them.

As for what they hold to, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one morning wearing a striped cloak of black wool, sat down, and then Fatima came and he admitted her into it, then ʿAli came and he admitted him, then al-Hasan and al-Husayn came and he admitted them too, and then said, "God only desires to remove from you the defilement, O people of the household," it only indicates that they are among the people of the household, not that others are not. And even if its indication were granted to include that, it would not be counted, because it stands in opposition to the explicit text.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 34:

﴿And remember what is recited in your houses﴾ That is: mention to the people, by way of admonition and reminder, what is recited in your houses.

﴿of the verses of Allah and the wisdom﴾ from the Book, which combines being the clear verses of Allah that indicate the truthfulness of prophethood by its inimitable composition, and being wisdom comprising the various sciences and laws. This is a reminder of the blessing He bestowed upon them in making them the people of the House of Prophethood and the place of descent of revelation, and of what they witnessed of the hardships of revelation, which necessitates strength of faith and eagerness for obedience, as an incitement to refrain and to comply with what they have been charged with. The mention of recitation "in the houses" rather than descent "in them" — although descent would be more fitting given that they are the place of descent of revelation — is because recitation is general, covering all the verses and occurring in every house, and because of its repetition, which necessitates their being able to remember and to remind, unlike descent. And the reciter is not specified, so that it includes the recitation of Gabriel and the recitation of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon them both, and their recitation and the recitation of others, by way of teaching and learning.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Subtle, Acquainted﴾ He knows and arranges what is good in the religion, and for this reason He does what He does of commanding and forbidding; or He knows who is fit for prophethood and who deserves to be of the People of His House.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 35:

﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ i.e., those who enter into submission (al-silm) and yield to the judgment of God Most High, both males and females.

﴿and the believing men and the believing women﴾ who affirm what must be affirmed (p-104) of the two groups, ﴿and the devoutly obedient men and the devoutly obedient women﴾ who persist in obedience and perform it.

﴿and the truthful men and the truthful women﴾ in speech and deed; ﴿and the patient men and the patient women﴾ in obedience and in refraining from sins.

﴿and the humble men and the humble women﴾ who are humble before God with their hearts and their limbs.

﴿and the almsgiving men and the almsgiving women﴾ with what is obligatory upon their wealth.

﴿and the fasting men and the fasting women﴾ who observe the obligatory fast.

﴿and the men and women who guard their private parts﴾ from what is unlawful.

﴿and the men and women who remember God much﴾ with their hearts and their tongues.

﴿God has prepared for them﴾ in return for the good deeds of those mentioned ﴿forgiveness﴾ for the minor sins they have committed, because these good deeds expiate them; ﴿and a great reward﴾ for what proceeded from them of acts of obedience and signs. It is a promise to them and to those like them for obedience and for adorning themselves with these praiseworthy qualities.

It is related that the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), may God be pleased with them, said: "O Messenger of God, God has mentioned the men in the Qur'an with goodness, so is there no good among us by which we are mentioned? Indeed, we fear that no obedience of ours will be accepted," and so this was revealed. It is also said that the questioner was Umm Salama. It is further related that when what was revealed concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed, the women of the believers said: "Has nothing been revealed concerning us?" and so this was revealed. The conjunction of the females with the males is due to the difference of the two genders, and it is necessary. As for the conjunction of the pair with the pair, it is due to the difference of the two attributes, so it is not necessary; for this reason it was omitted in God's saying ﴿Muslim women, believing women﴾. Its purpose is to indicate that the basis for preparing what has been prepared for them is their combining these beautiful attributes.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 33, verse 36:**

﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman﴾ That is: it is not right nor proper for a man or a woman among the believers.

﴿when God and His Messenger have decided a matter﴾ That is: when the Messenger of God has decided. God, exalted is He, is mentioned to magnify his command (ﷺ), or to indicate that his decision (ﷺ) is the decision of God, Mighty and Majestic. It was revealed concerning Zaynab bint Jahsh, the daughter of his paternal aunt Umaymah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) proposed her for Zayd ibn Harithah, but she and her brother 'Abd Allah refused. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who had offered herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), so he married her to Zayd. She and her brother were displeased and said: "We only wanted God and His Messenger, yet he married us to his servant."

﴿they have no choice in their affair﴾ That they should choose from their affair whatever they wish. Rather, it is obligatory upon them to make their opinion follow his opinion (ﷺ), and their choice follow his choice. The two pronouns are in the plural because "believing man" and "believing woman" are general, since both occur in the context of negation (siyaq al-nafy). It is also said that the second pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the plural is for magnification. It is read as (تَكُونَ) with a ta' (feminine form of the verb).

﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger﴾ in any matter, acting in it according to his own opinion, ﴿has certainly strayed﴾ from the path of truth, ﴿into manifest error﴾ That is: clearly deviating from the ways of rightness.

﴿وَإذْ تَقُولُ﴾ i.e., remember the time when you said.

﴿لِلَّذِي أنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ﴾ by His granting him guidance to Islam, and your granting him (guidance) to good upbringing and care for him. (p-105)

﴿وَأنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ by acting upon what Allah enabled you to do of the various kinds of kindness, among which is his manumission. He was Zayd ibn Harithah. Mentioning him with the aforementioned title serves to show the incompatibility of his situation with what came from him (ﷺ) of displaying what was contrary to what was in his heart, since that (concealment) occurs only out of shyness (istihya') or modesty (ihtishām), and both of these are inconceivable in the case of Zayd.

﴿أمْسِكْ عَلَيْكَ زَوْجَكَ﴾ i.e., Zaynab. This is because he (ﷺ) saw her after he had married her to him, and a natural feeling arose in his heart, of the sort that humans can hardly be free from. So he said: "Glory be to Allah, the Turner of hearts." Zaynab heard this glorification and mentioned it to Zayd, and he became aware of it, and a dislike of her company entered his heart. So he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I want to separate from my companion." He said: "What is the matter with you? Has something from her made you doubtful?" He said: "No, by Allah, I have seen from her nothing but good, but she is haughty towards me because of her nobility." So he said to him: "Keep your wife for yourself."

﴿وَاتَّقِ اللَّهَ﴾ regarding her, so do not divorce her out of harm and under the pretext of her arrogance.

﴿وَتُخْفِي في نَفْسِكَ ما اللَّهُ مُبْدِيهِ﴾ namely, marrying her if he divorced her, or the desire to divorce her.

﴿وَتَخْشى النّاسَ﴾ their reproach of you for it.

﴿واللَّهُ أحَقُّ أنْ تَخْشاهُ﴾ if there is anything to be feared. The "waw" here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the reproach is not for concealment alone, but for concealment out of fear of people's talk, and for displaying what is contrary to what is concealed within. In such matters the better course is to remain silent, or to entrust the matter to one's Lord.

﴿فَلَمّا قَضى زَيْدٌ مِنها وطَرًا﴾ to the point that he had no further need of her, and he divorced her, and her waiting period (iddah) ended. It was said: "The fulfilment of need (qada' al-watar) is a euphemism (kinaya) for divorce, like saying: 'I have no need of you.'"

﴿زَوَّجْناكَها﴾ It was also recited as: (زَوَّجْتُكَها). The meaning is the command to marry her to him (ﷺ). It was said: He made her his wife without an intermediary contract. This is supported by the fact that she used to say to the other wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah Most High arranged my marriage, while your guardians married you off." It was also said: Zayd was the envoy in her proposal, and that was a great trial, and (also) a witness of justice, by the strength of his faith.

﴿لِكَيْ لا يَكُونَ عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ حَرَجٌ﴾ narrowness and hardship.

﴿فِي أزْواجِ أدْعِيائِهِمْ﴾ i.e., regarding the marriage of their wives.

﴿إذا قَضَوْا مِنهُنَّ وطَرًا﴾ for they have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example. This indicates that his ruling (ﷺ) and the ruling for the community are the same, except what the evidence specifically exempts.

﴿وَكانَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ i.e., what He wills to bring into existence of matters, or His specific command "Be!"

﴿مَفْعُولا﴾ brought into being without doubt. This is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiradh tadhyili) confirming what came before it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 38:

﴿There is no restriction upon the Prophet in what Allah has ordained for him﴾. That is: it is not correct, nor is it consistent with wisdom, that there should be constraint upon him.

﴿in what Allah has ordained for him﴾. That is: He allotted for him and decreed it, from the expression "faradha lahu fi al-diwan kadha" (he assigned him such-and-such in the register). From this comes the term "furud al-'asakir" (the assigned stipends of the troops) for their allowances.

﴿the way of Allah﴾ is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun (masdar), like their saying "turaban wa jandalan" (dust and gravel), emphasizing what precedes it concerning the negation of restriction. That is: Allah has established this as a practice (sunnah).

﴿with those who passed away﴾, that is, who went before, ﴿from before﴾, from among the Prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, in that He granted them latitude in matters of marriage and otherwise. Indeed, David, upon him be peace, had one hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and Solomon, upon him be peace, had three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the command of Allah is a decree determined﴾ means: a decree decreed, and a judgment definitively settled. It is a parenthetical clause inserted between the two relative clauses that function as a single unit, for the sake of hastening to affirm and confirm the negation of restriction.

(p-106) ﴿Alladhina yuballighuna risalati Allah﴾ is a description (sifah) of "those who passed before," or a praise (madh) for them, in the accusative or the nominative. It has also been read as "risalata Allah" (in the singular).

﴿Wa yakhshawnahu﴾ in everything they do and leave undone, especially in the matter of conveying the Message, where they do not omit a single letter of it, and the blame of any blamer does not take them in that.

﴿Wa la yakhshawna ahadan illa Allah﴾ In describing them as restricting fear to Allah the Exalted, there is an allusion (ta'ridh) to what proceeded from him (ﷺ) of guarding against the censure of people, after the explicit statement in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾.

﴿Wa kafa billahi hasiba﴾ sufficient (kafiyan) for all fears, so that none other than Him should be feared; or one who takes account (muhasiban) of the small and the great, so that the true fear of Him, the Exalted, is obligatory.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 33, verse 40:

﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men﴾ That is: in actual reality, so that between him and them there would be established what is established between a father and his son, such as the prohibition of marriage by affinity (ḥurmat al-muṣāharah) and other things. His general application is not undermined by his being the father of al-Ṭāhir, al-Qāsim and Ibrahim, for they did not reach puberty; and had they reached puberty, they would have been men belonging to him ﷺ, not to them.

﴿But he is the Messenger of Allah﴾ That is: he was a messenger of Allah, and every messenger is the father of his community, but not in actual reality. Rather, it means that he is compassionate and sincere toward them, and a cause of their everlasting life. Zayd was only one of your men with whom he has no blood relationship, so his ruling is their ruling. Adoption and claiming (as a son) have no ruling other than closeness and special association.

﴿And the Seal of the Prophets﴾ That is: he was their last, the one with whom they were sealed. It was also read with a kasra on the ta' (khātim), meaning that he was their seal (the one who seals them), and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports this. [It reads:] "But a prophet who sealed the prophets." And in either case, had he had a son who reached puberty, that son would have been a prophet, and he ﷺ would not have been the Seal of the Prophets. As it is narrated that he said about Ibrahim when he died: "Had he lived, he would have been a prophet." Nor does the descent of Jesus after him, peace be upon them both, undermine this, because the meaning of his being the Seal of the Prophets is that no one will be made a prophet after him, and Jesus is among those who were made prophets before him. When he descends, he will descend acting upon the law of Muhammad ﷺ, praying towards his qibla, as if he were one of his community.
